---
title: "Research"
---

My research agenda examines the **political economy of energy and climate**: how physical infrastructure — its failures, its expansion, and the institutions that regulate it — shapes voting behavior and democratic accountability. Methodologically, I work with causal inference designs (difference-in-differences, panel methods), spatial data and GIS, survey experiments, and statistical machine learning, almost entirely in R.

## Working papers

::: {.paper-entry}
[Power Outages and Voting Behavior in São Paulo]{.paper-title}

[Working paper]{.status-badge}

Widespread storm-induced blackouts in the São Paulo metropolitan region left millions of residents without power for days. This paper estimates the duration of blackout exposure at the district level — using population-weighted areal interpolation across 27,000+ census tracts — and identifies its electoral ramifications with two-way fixed effects and difference-in-differences designs, including heterogeneous effects in high-vulnerability districts.

::: {.paper-entry}
[Do Electricity Regulators Face Voter Backlash over AI Data Centers?]{.paper-title}

[In progress]{.status-badge}

Do voters who live near AI data centers turn out at higher rates — and punish incumbents — in the elections that regulate their electricity? This mixed-method project studies the 2025 Georgia Public Service Commission elections, combining a spatially weighted difference-in-differences design using observational returns with a conjoint survey experiment to test the mechanisms behind voter backlash.

## Other research interests

**Comparative climate politics.** I am broadly interested in how democracies manage the distributive politics of the energy transition — cross-national variation in climate policy ambition, expert and public opinion on climate policy instruments, and the political geography of energy infrastructure siting.

**Earlier work.** My M.A. thesis analyzed Swedish forest policy conflicts using content analysis and process tracing, examining how competing framings of sustainability shaped policy outcomes in European climate and forest governance.

## Methods

Causal inference (DiD, two-way fixed effects, panel data) · spatial analysis and GIS (areal interpolation, spatial weighting) · survey and conjoint experiments · text analysis · statistical machine learning · data visualization (ggplot2, ArcGIS)
